notes: Interlocutory TCC judgment on strike-out of £6.7m damages figure; adjourned with case-management orders.

enrichment.short_title: Plymco v ASM: strike-out application over QS damages breakdown
key_facts: Plymouth South West Co-Operative Society claimed about £3 million against architect ASM for breach of contract and negligence over refurbishment of its Derry's Cross store in Plymouth.
The claim rested on a notional reasonable cost of £6.7 million against actual outturn costs of £8.6 million for works that could have been managed differently.

Claimant QS expert Mr Jervis provided the only breakdown of the £6.7 million figure in Appendix K of his report, but answers to Part 35 questions in June 2004 gave no calculable justification for key line items.
Judge Seymour QC had earlier found the Scott Schedule inadequate; Judge Coulson adjourned rather than struck out the damages figure pending amended pleadings and a Part 35 experts' note.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Interlocutory application in the Technology and Construction Court to strike out the £6.7 million damages figure or debar the claimant's QS expert from giving evidence on sections 10 and 11 of his report.
enrichment.outcome: Strike-out application adjourned to 7 January 2005; claimant ordered to amend pleadings by 17 December 2004 with a pleaded breakdown of the notional £6.7 million cost and experts to produce a Part 35 note by 23 December 2004.
enrichment.ratio: Where a claimant's expert fails adequately to particularise a central damages figure after court orders and judicial warnings, the case may be in serious difficulty, but strike-out is inappropriate without evidence from the opposing expert that prejudice prevents response; the overriding objective favours adjournment and targeted case management over immediate debarring.
legal_issues: Whether inadequate answers to Part 35 questions justified debarring the claimant's QS expert or striking out the £6.7 million damages figure
Whether Appendix K could support the pleaded reasonable cost figure given bald or unparticularised line items
Whether the defendant's expert had shown sufficient prejudice from the claimant's failure to provide calculations
What case-management orders were appropriate before trial fixed for March 2005

confidence.notes: Interlocutory orders and reasoning on expert particularisation are explicit, though final trial outcome is not recorded.

notes: Detailed Chancery trial on 1930s Becontree Estate covenants; benefit, burden and pre-emption fully analysed.

enrichment.short_title: UEL v Barking councils: Becontree Campus restrictive covenants
key_facts: Between 1931 and 1946 the LCC conveyed the Barking Campus to Essex County Council for educational use subject to user, approval and pre-emption covenants protecting the Becontree municipal housing estate.
UEL, successor to Essex, wished to sell the surplus campus for housing but LBBD and LBR contended they could enforce the covenants and demand substantial consideration for consent.
Third-defendant tenants and private owners on the estate were joined but held not entitled to enforce the restrictive covenants.
UEL argued unity of seisin extinguished the covenants when LBBD briefly held both dominant and servient land for different statutory purposes.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Part 8 claim for declarations on construction, validity and enforceability of historic restrictive covenants and the identity of beneficiaries and burdened owners.
enrichment.outcome: Covenants held valid and subsisting; benefit vested in LBBD and LBR and burden on UEL; UEL may sell at full market value free of user and approval covenants but must first offer pre-emption to LBBD and LBR acting together at market value free of those restrictions.
enrichment.ratio: On their true construction the 1930s conveyances confine covenant benefit to the LCC and statutory successors to its housing functions on the Becontree Estate, bind only statutory successors to Essex's education functions, and are not extinguished by unity of seisin where the same authority holds dominant and servient land for different statutory purposes.
legal_issues: Whether tenants and private owners could enforce the restrictive covenants
Whether the pre-emption covenant created an interest in land or passed by transfer orders to LBBD and LBR
Whether section 78 effected annexation of covenant benefit to the Becontree Estate
Whether unity of seisin extinguished covenants when LBBD held both campus and housing land
linked_authorities: Crest Nicholson Residential (South) Ltd v McAllister [2004] EWCA Civ 410
Prescott v Birmingham Corp [1955] 1 Ch 910
Pritchard v Briggs [1980] Ch 338

confidence.notes: Comprehensive declaratory judgment with clear holdings on each covenant and vesting issue.

notes: Court of Appeal dismisses Yardley's challenges to harassment injunction, committal and draft judgment procedure.

enrichment.short_title: Birmingham Council v Yardley: harassment injunction and committal appeal
key_facts: Mr Yardley disputed Birmingham City Council's refusal to renew his hackney carriage licences from the early 1990s and sent 1,626 repetitive letters between 1993 and 2002 targeting council officers and licensing chairman Brian Nott.
Mr Recorder Tedd QC dismissed Yardley's misfeasance counterclaim, found nuisance proved, and granted an injunction restricting correspondence after a trial in October 2002.
HH Judge McKenna sentenced Yardley to 28 days' suspended imprisonment for breach, discharged the original injunction and made a narrower replacement limiting him to one letter per month.
Yardley argued the draft judgment handed down on 8 January 2003 was invalid and raised bias because the recorder and council counsel shared chambers.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal as of right against committal and applications for permission to appeal against a replacement injunction and refusal to pronounce judgment in open court.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed and permission applications refused with costs; court held the draft judgment was validly handed down, the injunction balanced Article 10 rights, and any chambers objection had been waived at trial.
enrichment.ratio: A judgment headed 'Draft' and handed down in open court is not invalid merely because it awaits final approval; an injunction restraining repetitive harassment of a public authority may be proportionate under Articles 6, 10 and 11; shared chambers without objection at trial does not establish bias under Locabail principles.
legal_issues: Whether handing down a draft judgment without formal pronouncement invalidated subsequent injunction and committal proceedings
Whether the injunction breached Yardley's Convention rights to freedom of expression
Whether apparent bias arose from the recorder and counsel being members of the same chambers
Whether committal and replacement injunction orders were procedurally irregular
linked_authorities: Locabail (UK) Ltd v Bayfield Properties Ltd [2000] QB 451

confidence.notes: Appellate disposition on all grounds is clearly reasoned against a detailed factual background.

notes: Leading damages appeal on collateral warranty measure; continuing-loss multiplier approach overturned.

enrichment.short_title: Salford Council v Torkington: measure of damages for shop competition warranty
key_facts: Salford City Council assured shop tenants Torkington and Darby that no competing grocer or off-licence would open on the Hay Mill Estate before they took assignment and a new lease of 180 Cleggs Lane.
Rival shops at 2 Hay Mill Avenue and 300 Cleggs Lane opened with off-licences, profits fell from about £17,000 to £2,000 and the business closed on 14 February 1988.
The council claimed rent arrears and forfeiture; the tenants counterclaimed for breach of collateral warranties and set off damages.
Judge Kershaw awarded about £401,000 including future loss to a notional 1994 sale, but the council conceded forfeiture would fail once damages exceeded rent.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from assessment of damages following liability trial on counterclaim for breach of collateral contractual warranties relating to competition assurances.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; damages under bands 5 and 6 reduced to £65,000 as at March 1988, representing the value of the business as a going concern but for the breaches, with consequential interest and costs adjustments to be agreed.
enrichment.ratio: Where collateral warranties induce acquisition of a business lease and breach renders the business worthless at closure, the normal contractual measure is the difference between the value as warranted and actual value at the reasonable cut-off when the tenants ceased trading, not a speculative continuing multiplier/multiplicand assessment of profits to a later notional sale.
legal_issues: Whether future loss after business closure should be assessed on a continuing basis or capitalised at closure
Whether a multiplier/multiplicand approach required a loss-of-chance discount for lawful competition and neighbourhood decline
Whether the tenants' decision to sell in 1987 limited recoverable continuing profits
What value of the business as at March 1988 should be adopted from competing expert evidence
linked_authorities: Allied Maples Group Ltd v Simmons & Simmons [1995] 1 WLR 1602
ELO Entertainments Ltd v Grand Metropolitan Retailing Ltd [1999] 1 All ER (Comm) 473
Royscot Trust Ltd v Rogerson [1991] 2 QB 297

confidence.notes: Court of Appeal's principled ruling on measure of damages is explicit though final interest figures were left for agreement.

notes: Criminal appeal partly succeeds on confiscation valuation and costs; sentence upheld.

enrichment.short_title: R v Davies: employee theft sentence and confiscation appeal
key_facts: Davies, traffic manager of Coombes Travel, pleaded guilty to nine counts of theft and 72 offences were taken into consideration for stealing about £35,400 from Friday coach-trip cash over several years.
He was sentenced to two years' imprisonment concurrent, with a confiscation order of £156,000 and two years consecutive in default, plus £10,000 prosecution costs.
Marked-note evidence showed cash collected from tourists never reached company accounts; he had previous good character but lived beyond his £24,000 salary through gambling and holidays.
Post-sentencing evidence showed the family home had been overvalued at £372,000 rather than £275,000 and sale costs had not been deducted.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal with leave against two-year theft sentence, confiscation order and prosecution costs order following guilty pleas in Bristol Crown Court.
enrichment.outcome: Two-year sentence upheld as not manifestly excessive; confiscation order reduced from £156,000 to £105,500 after corrected house valuation and deductable sale costs; prosecution costs order set aside; default term unchanged.
enrichment.ratio: A two-year sentence for breach-of-trust theft of about £35,000 on a late plea falls within the accepted tariff; confiscation must be based on up-to-date professional property valuation at the hearing date with sale costs deducted; prosecution costs should not be ordered where the defendant lacks means to pay within a reasonable period.
legal_issues: Whether two years' imprisonment was manifestly excessive for trusted employee theft
Whether the confiscation order reflected an accurate valuation of the defendant's realisable assets
Whether estate agents' and solicitors' sale costs should be deducted from property value
Whether the prosecution costs order was lawful given the defendant's means
linked_authorities: R v Lemmon (1991) 13 Cr App R (S) 66
R v Kramer (1992) 13 Cr App R (S) 390
R v Nottingham JJ, ex parte Fohman (1987) 84 Cr App R 316

confidence.notes: Appellate conclusions on sentence, confiscation arithmetic and costs are clearly stated.

notes: Authoritative Part 36 late-acceptance discretion judgment; appeal dismissed.

enrichment.short_title: Capital Bank v Stickland: late acceptance of claimant's Part 36 offer
key_facts: Capital Bank sued mortgagee Stickland for delivery up or value of the vessel CATABATIC, offering £85,000 inclusive of interest by Part 36 offer on 10 June 2003.

Stickland did not accept within 21 days, flouted inspection orders, and only sought to accept on the morning of trial on 27 February 2004 after a surveyor found hull identification evidence undermining his defence.
Judge Kershaw refused late acceptance, proceeded to trial and awarded £97,088.80 with indemnity costs and 10% interest on costs from 1 July 2003.
Stickland offered no security for payment and his main defence that the mortgaged vessel differed from the subject vessel collapsed after inspection in Portugal.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal with permission against refusal to allow late acceptance of a claimant's Part 36 offer and against indemnity costs and enhanced interest on costs.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; court held the judge had a broad discretion to refuse late acceptance where new evidence strengthened the claim, the application was made on the trial date and the defendant offered no ready payment.
enrichment.ratio: CPR Part 36 does not require a claimant to withdraw or reduce an offer as a condition of opposing late acceptance; the court has wide discretion informed by change of circumstance, timing of the application and availability of the defendant's money, following Cumper v Pothecary and Garner v Cleggs principles.
legal_issues: Whether refusal of late Part 36 acceptance is limited to cases of substantial change of circumstance
Whether a claimant must withdraw his offer before opposing late acceptance
Whether new survey evidence justified refusing permission to accept after 21 days
Whether indemnity costs and 10% interest on costs were properly awarded after refusal of late acceptance
linked_authorities: Cumper v Pothecary [1941] 2 KB 58
Garner v Cleggs [1983] 1 WLR 862
Flynn v Scougall [2004] EWCA Civ 873
Scammell v Dicker [2001] 1 WLR 651

confidence.notes: Central Part 36 discretion issue and costs consequences are comprehensively reasoned by the full court.

notes: Permission refused against two-year civil restraint order in long-running ancillary relief litigation.

enrichment.short_title: Foenander: civil restraint order in repeated ancillary relief litigation

statutes_considered.title: Inheritance (Provision for Family and Dependants) Act 1975

key_facts: Mr Foenander failed to pay a £30,000 lump sum ordered in December 1994 after ancillary relief proceedings upheld on appeal through Singer J and the Court of Appeal by 1997.

From 2002 he repeatedly applied to set aside district judge Maple's order alleging non-disclosure, forged documents and judicial conspiracy, applications dismissed by district judges Brasse and Maple.
The President made a two-year civil restraint order on 24 March 2004 forbidding further applications relating to the marriage or financial relief, excluding bankruptcy and enforcement proceedings.
Coleridge J amended the order under the slip rule to clarify it covered pursuit of outstanding applications and dismissed a stale permission appeal against a costs judge's order.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Applications for permission to appeal against a civil restraint order made by the President of the Family Division and a subsequent slip-rule amendment by Coleridge J.
enrichment.outcome: Permission to appeal refused on both orders; Wall LJ held the restraint order was justified to stop meritless attempts to reopen a finally determined 1994 order and Coleridge J's amendment reflected the President's stated intention.
enrichment.ratio: A civil restraint order may properly be made where a litigant persistently seeks to relitigate a finally determined ancillary relief order without realistic prospect of success; the CPR slip rule may amend an order to give effect to the court's intention, and dismissal of permission to appeal a costs judge's order is final with no further appeal to the Court of Appeal.
legal_issues: Whether a civil restraint order was properly made without formal summons or Attorney General intervention
Whether missing court documents vitiated proceedings for natural justice reasons
Whether Coleridge J validly used the slip rule to extend the restraint to outstanding applications
Whether the court had jurisdiction to entertain a permission appeal against Costs Judge Simons' order
linked_authorities: Bristol-Myers Squibb v Baker Norton Pharmaceuticals [2001] EWCA Civ 414
Riniker v University College London [2001] 1 WLR 13
Grepe v Loam (1887) 37 Ch D 168

notes: Neuberger J revokes permission to appeal after respondent denied skeleton; affirmation point decisive.

enrichment.short_title: Eid v Al-Kazemi: revocation of permission on share-sale affirmation
key_facts: Mr Eid sued Mrs Al-Kazemi to enforce agreements for transfer of Ramelle Investments Corporation shares, originally for £350,000 later varied to £400,000 and reverted to £350,000.
Deputy judge Martin QC found an agreement existed, rejected undue influence on the facts, held affirmation estopped rescission and ordered specific performance.
Neuberger J initially granted permission to appeal on undue influence and affirmation after the judge had not been referred to Maclan v Dowsett.
In October 2003 Mrs Al-Kazemi accepted about £160,000 from Eid knowing he believed it completed the purchase price while intending to treat it as loan repayment.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application to reconsider and revoke grant of permission to appeal after the respondent had not been supplied with the appellant's skeleton argument before the original permission decision.
enrichment.outcome: Permission to appeal revoked; court held affirmation or estoppel plainly precluded Mrs Al-Kazemi from setting aside the agreement even assuming undue influence on earlier variations.
enrichment.ratio: Where a party free of undue influence accepts substantial payments knowing the other believes they complete contractual obligations under a share purchase agreement, equitable affirmation or estoppel may prevent later rescission for earlier undue influence; failure to provide a requested skeleton before permission is granted requires reconsideration of permission.
legal_issues: Whether permission to appeal should be revoked because the respondent was not given the appellant's skeleton
Whether Mrs Al-Kazemi affirmed the July 2003 share agreement by accepting £140,000 and a Mercedes in October 2003
Whether deceitful treatment of payments as loan repayment prevented rescission for undue influence
Whether specific performance should follow if affirmation was established
linked_authorities: Maclan v Dowsett (unreported, 14 June 2004)

confidence.notes: Final procedural order revoking permission is clear; underlying trial findings are summarised but not revisited on merits.

notes: Case stated appeal on public place; magistrates' conviction upheld.

enrichment.short_title: R v Lewis: pub car park as public place for drink driving
key_facts: Mr Lewis was seen driving in the Black Bull public house car park in Hillingdon at 18:35 during licensing hours on 2 June 2003.
Police stopped him in the car park and a breath test at Uxbridge police station recorded 75 micrograms of alcohol per 100 millilitres of breath.
He argued no positive evidence showed the car park was a 'public place' and that inference alone was insufficient.
The magistrates convicted him; after special reasons he was fined £200 and disqualified for three years.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal by way of case stated from Uxbridge magistrates asking whether the Black Bull car park was a public place for section 5 Road Traffic Act 1988 purposes.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; High Court answered yes, holding magistrates were bound to find a public house car park during licensing hours a public place on the primary facts without evidence of actual users.
enrichment.ratio: A car park attached to a public house open during licensing hours is a public place for section 5 purposes because the publican invites patrons to use it; it is sufficient that the place is one to which the public are invited and may properly be inferred to use, following Elkins v Cartlidge, Pugh v Knipe and Sandy v Martin.
legal_issues: Whether the prosecution had to adduce evidence of actual public use of the car park
Whether magistrates could properly infer a pub car park was a public place during licensing hours
How R v Spence on dangerous driving in a private office car park applied to pub car parks
linked_authorities: Elkins v Cartlidge [1947] 1 All ER 829
Pugh v Knipe [1972] RTR 286
Sandy v Martin [1974] RTR 236
R v Colin Michael Spence (unreported, 23 March 1999)

notes: Judicial review on NHS injury benefit calculation; 1995 regulations applied, claim dismissed.

enrichment.short_title: Malekout v SSH: NHS injury benefit average remuneration date

statutes_considered.title: National Health Service Pension Scheme Regulations 1995

key_facts: Dr Malekout, an NHS practitioner, claimed permanent injury benefit after ceasing employment on 16 December 1990 following a workplace injury.
He had earlier received temporary allowance under regulation 4(5) while on leave with reduced emoluments from 22 January 1987.

The Secretary of State calculated average remuneration under the 1995 regulations using the yearly average of uprated earnings to December 1990, producing a lower benefit than if the 1987 reduction date were used.
The claimant never served written notice under regulation 23 opting into the 1974 regulations; the regimes differ only marginally on uprating mechanics.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of the Secretary of State for Health's determination of permanent injury benefit under the NHS Injury Benefits Regulations.
enrichment.outcome: Claim dismissed; Wilkie J held the 1995 regulations applied, the claimant was a practitioner under regulation 2(1)(b), and the deemed retirement date for average remuneration was 16 December 1990 under regulation 2(1)(b)(iii) not January 1987.
enrichment.ratio: Without a regulation 23 written election the 1995 NHS Injury Benefits Regulations govern; for a practitioner eligible under regulation 4(2) average remuneration is the yearly average of uprated earnings calculated as if retirement occurred on the date employment ceased by reason of injury, even if that yields less than the prior temporary allowance under regulation 4(5).
legal_issues: Whether the 1974 or 1995 injury benefit regulations applied absent a regulation 23 notice
Whether average remuneration for a practitioner should use final year's pensionable pay or uprated earnings average
Whether the calculation end date was the emoluments reduction in 1987 or employment cessation in 1990
Whether the drop from temporary to permanent benefit created an unintended anomaly requiring a different construction

confidence.notes: Core statutory construction and outcome are clear though the published judgment extract begins mid-reasoning on regulation 23.
